verses.1: Al-Mizan distinguishes ishtikāʾ, manifesting one’s own misfortune, from shikāya, complaining of another’s hateful act, and taḥāwur, reciprocal dialogue or dispute. The verse arose when an Anṣārī woman whose husband pronounced the pre-Islamic ẓihār formula—‘you are to me like my mother’s back’—asked the Prophet for a way to restore the marriage. In the first ‘God heard,’ hearing is metonymy for accepting and answering her plea; in the last, it has its ordinary meaning of hearing both disputants. God therefore answered her grief under this pagan practice while hearing every voice and seeing with perfect insight.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says ẓihār does not make a wife a mother, annul a marriage, or impose the pre-Islamic permanent prohibition claimed for it: only women who gave birth are mothers. The formula is a legally rejected, hateful falsehood, contrary both to the Sharīʿa and reality. Nevertheless, a husband who invokes it and wishes to resume intercourse must first discharge kaffāra, since marriage remains but intercourse is barred until expiation. God’s pardoning forgiveness shows it is sinful but forgivable, apparently conditional on kaffāra in light of the following verses and (58:4).
verses.3: Al-Mizan reads the verse as conditional: the man who has pronounced ẓihār and intends to revoke its formula by resuming intercourse must free a captive before touching his wife. ‘Go back on what they said’ is this intended return, not merely regret, though regret follows from it; it is not a second repetition of the formula, since Prophetic practice makes kaffāra depend on the occurrence of ẓihār, not its number. The command is divine admonition grounded in God’s knowledge, and kaffāra removes the adverse consequence of the deed.
verses.4: Al-Mizan sets the second and third forms of ẓihār kaffāra: one unable to free a captive must fast two consecutive months before intercourse, and one unable to fast must feed sixty needy people. Repeating the condition before touching removes any claim that it applies only to the first form. These rules preserve the marriage while penalizing the pagan custom so people accept God’s and His Messenger’s judgment and reject false norms. They are God’s ḥudūd, boundaries not to be transgressed; disbelief here most apparently means rejecting the ruling and treating ẓihār as valid, though it may mean practical rebellious disobedience.
verses.5: Al-Mizan defines muḥādda as dissension and opposition, and kabt as being humiliated, subdued, and debased. The verse continues the warning not to violate God’s limits: those opposing God and His Messenger will be disgraced as earlier opponents were. Clear communications establish that the message is from God and the Messenger truthful, while those who disbelieve in and reject them receive humiliating punishment.
verses.6: Al-Mizan makes the universal resurrection and disclosure of deeds the time at which the disbelievers’ painful punishment occurs. God’s iḥṣāʾ is complete, comprehensive enumeration from which nothing is lost, a term associated with counting by pebbles. He has recorded deeds they forgot, and His witness over everything explains that perfect record.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads the opening question as al-istifhām al-inkāriy, a rebuking interrogation that demands certain knowledge of Allah's all-encompassing knowledge. Al-najwā is secret, intimate conversation; His being the fourth of three and sixth of five, with ‘less’ and ‘more’ encompassing every number, means His awareness of what is confided. This is al-maʿiyya al-ʿilmiyya, knowledge-based accompaniment, or al-maʿiyya al-wujūdiyya: wherever such people are, God is present as Hearing and Knowing. It is not bodily or spatial accompaniment, numerical addition, or confinement to a place. Thus it does not conflict with the denial of trinitarian number in (5:73): His oneness is al-wiḥda al-aḥadiyya, peerless uniqueness, not al-wiḥda al-ʿadadiyya, numerical oneness. He will disclose their deeds, including their secret counsels, at the Resurrection; the ending both explains this judgment by His knowledge and threatens what follows.
verses.8: Al-Mizan identifies those repeatedly returning to forbidden secret counsels as hypocrites and believers sick at heart, who sought to grieve the believers and opposed the Messenger. Addressing the Prophet about them rather than addressing them directly intensifies their contemptibility; yaʿūdūna indicates persistence, and saying they return to what they were forbidden rather than simply ‘to it’ makes the prohibition itself the ground of blame. The commentary distinguishes al-ithm, a sin whose evil remains with its doer and concerns God's right, from al-ʿudwān, harmful wrongdoing against others; both are divine disobedience. Maʿṣiyat al-rasūl is disobeying the Messenger's community-directed command in an otherwise permissible matter, such as a prohibition of secret converse, by virtue of his leadership and guardianship. Al-Mizan holds that the Jews are not explicitly included, despite the not-improbable report that Jews greeted the Prophet with al-sāmu ʿalayka, ‘death be upon you,’ while feigning al-salāmu ʿalayka; the rebuked group should therefore remain the hypocrites and sick at heart. Their inward question, ‘Why does Allah not punish us?’, is concealed rebellious sarcasm that effectively denies his messengership: were he God's Messenger, they suppose, God would punish their greeting. The reading that it means conversation among themselves is judged far-fetched. Hell refutes their presumption, and the commentary connects their refusal to desist with the later warning in (33:60) and (33:61).
verses.9: Al-Mizan says believers may hold private counsel, but only for birr, extensive good deeds, and taqwā, God-consciousness, rather than sin, hostility, and disobedience to the Messenger. Birr contrasts with al-ʿudwān and taqwā with al-ithm. The final reminder that all will be gathered to Allah makes their God-consciousness comprehensive.
verses.10: Al-Mizan takes al-najwā here to mean the secret counsels of hypocrites and those sick at heart, made attractive by Satan so that believers would be alarmed, imagine calamity, and grieve. God consoles believers that neither Satan nor these counsels can harm them except by His permission. They must therefore rely on Him, for whoever trusts Allah finds Him sufficient (65:3), and such reliance belongs to faith.
verses.11: Al-Mizan explains al-tafassuḥ as making an assembly spacious for another; although prompted by crowding in the Prophet's gathering, the etiquette is general, and Allah's making room means making room in Paradise. Al-nushūz, rising from a gathering, means yielding one's place to honor someone superior in knowledge and piety. The verse consequently distinguishes the ordinary believer, whom Allah raises a degree, from the learned believer, whom He raises in degrees; knowledge brings greater nearness and honor, as (39:9) also indicates. Its closing warning confirms that Allah is aware of this conduct.
verses.12: Al-Mizan reads the charity before private consultation with the Messenger as an obligation for the wealthy. It was best for their souls and purer for their hearts because wealthy Muslims could monopolize private access and display special closeness, grieving the poor; charity to the poor instead joined hearts, stirred compassion, and removed rancor. The shift in dhālika briefly addresses the Prophet between two addresses to believers and delicately honors him. If one has nothing to give, the duty does not apply: Allah's forgiveness and mercy permit consultation without charity, while also show that the original imperative was binding on those able to give.
verses.13: Al-Mizan says this verse abrogates the prior charity requirement and sharply reproves the companions and believers for abandoning private consultation out of fear of spending. It reports that only ʿAlī consulted the Prophet privately, doing so ten times and giving charity each time, before the rule was cancelled. Al-ishfāq means fear or anxiety; it may concern giving wealth, or an omitted object may make it fear of poverty. The plural al-ṣadaqāt also suggests fear of the recurring requirement, not a single gift. Allah's turning to them with forgiveness proves their reluctance was disobedience, though pardoned. Prayer, alms, and obedience then replace the abrogated particular duty with renewed adherence to all divine commands, under Allah's full awareness.
verses.14: Al-Mizan identifies the people with whom Allah is angry as the Jews and the people who ally with them as hypocrites. In their outward, wavering state the hypocrites are neither believers nor Jews, as in (4:143); in reality, however, their alliance joins them to those whom they befriend, so this does not conflict with (5:51). The reversed-pronoun interpretation is judged remote. Their final false oath is their knowing lie that they are believers like the community.
verses.15: Al-Mizan glosses al-iʿdād as preparation and says Allah has prepared severe punishment because their deeds were evil. The imperfect expression for what they had been doing establishes their continuous persistence in that evil.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites use aymān, oaths, as a junnah, a shield against suspicion whenever their conduct unsettles believers. In doing so they themselves leave Islam, Allah's path, and turn others from it. Their recompense is an ʿadhāb muhīn, an abasing punishment of humiliation and dishonor.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says worldly enjoyment in wealth and children calls them to their wrongdoing, yet neither can save them from Allah's everlasting punishment. Since only He can save them, they should believe in and worship Him; otherwise they remain in the Fire.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says the hypocrites will swear falsely to Allah at the Resurrection just as they swear to believers in this world. Although realities will then be manifest, deeply ingrained traits reappear there: as they live, so they die and are raised. Their futile requests to return, leave the Fire, or dispute likewise belong to a Day of requital rather than action. ‘They think they have something’ may describe their worldly belief that oaths hide falsehood, or their resurrection-day manifestation of that trait; in either case Allah judges them liars and does not heed their oath.
verses.19: Al-Mizan defines al-istiḥwādh as Satan's taking possession, overcoming, and dominating them; having made them forget Allah's remembrance, they are Satan's losing party.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says opposition to Allah and His Messenger explains the opponents' loss: they must be among all creation's humiliated. Since all glory, power, and might belong to Allah, one who resists Him can have only utter abasement.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan takes Allah's kitābah as His decree and reads the promised victory of Him and His messengers in three connected ways. First, truth prevails in al-ḥujjah: human nature recognizes a truth made clear, even when passion or another obstacle prevents actual submission. Second, it prevails through al-taʾyīd al-ghaybiyy and God's judgment for truth, as the destruction of deniers in earlier communities illustrates ((23:44); (10:47)). Third, faith itself gives believers an unconditional resolve: whether killing or being killed, they count success, unlike those who defend a worldly aim only while self-preservation is secure.

Al-Mizan applies this last principle to the Messenger's victories despite the fluctuations of battle. Muslim expansion and unity ceased only when intentions were corrupted, God-consciousness and sincerity were exchanged for power and kingdom, and people changed themselves, as (8:53) states. Security upon the religion was conditioned on fearing Allah (5:3), and believers' ascendancy likewise remains conditioned by faith (3:139).
verses.22:
Al-Mizan says sincere faith in Allah and the Last Day cannot coexist with love or alliance for persistent opponents of Allah and His Messenger, even where kinship gives its strongest inducement to affection. Allah's inscribing faith in such hearts means establishing and confirming it so that it does not vanish. He strengthens them with a spirit from Himself; although some call it Gabriel, the Qur'an, proof, or knowledge, those readings lack literal evidence. The apparent meaning is an additional spirit of faith beyond the human spirit shared with disbelievers, giving a new life, power, and consciousness, like the light and good life described in (6:122), (16:97), and (57:28).

Al-Mizan rejects reducing this spirit to a figurative light of knowledge. This noble life leads to eternal happiness. Paradise, Allah's pleasure with their sincere faith, and their pleasure in His good life and Paradise follow; His pleasure means mercy. They are therefore ḥizbullāh, Allah's party, set against Satan's party, and are the prosperous.
